questions.q: Why does an agent still need undo and rollback strategies even with human approval checkpoints in place?
options: Because approval checkpoints are never actually effective
Because a human approving a request doesn't guarantee it was correct — the reviewer can misread the situation, or new information can surface after the action already ran
Because the Claude API requires every tool to have an undo function defined
Because audit logs cannot be created without an undo strategy
questions.explain: Approval catches many bad decisions before they execute, but it isn't infallible; undo and rollback exist for the case where an approved action still turns out to be wrong.

questions.q: What makes "true reversal" possible for an action like updating a database field?
options: True reversal is possible for every action with no special preparation needed
Capturing the prior ("before") state before writing the new value, so the undo can write that before-state back
Sending a second, unrelated transaction that happens to cancel out the first
True reversal only applies to actions that were rejected, never to ones that were approved
questions.explain: True reversal restores the exact prior state — which requires capturing that prior state before the change is made, so it can be written back later if needed.

questions.q: What is a "compensating action," using the wire transfer example from this lesson?
options: A way to retroactively make the original wire transfer never have happened
A second, different action (like a reversal transfer) that offsets the effect of an irreversible first action, without erasing that it happened
A setting that prevents wire transfers from ever being approved
The same thing as a true reversal, just under a different name
questions.explain: You can't un-send a wire transfer, but you can initiate a second transfer that reverses its financial effect — the audit trail needs to show both as linked, since the original event still happened.

questions.q: For an action like sending an email, which the lesson places in the "can't undo — only contain" category, what is the correct response to a mistaken send?
options: Notify affected people, document exactly what happened, and treat a stronger approval checkpoint on that tool as the real fix going forward
Attempt to silently delete the email from the recipient's inbox
Nothing can be done, so no action should be taken at all
Automatically send a second email claiming the first one never happened
questions.explain: A genuinely permanent action has no undo mechanism — the realistic response is damage control (notify, document) plus prevention (stronger approval gating) rather than pretending a rollback feature exists.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend doing with a tool's undo category (true reversal / compensating action / can't undo) before the tool is ever deployed to an agent?
options: Wait until the first real incident happens, then decide the category reactively
Classify it in advance, since that decision determines what "fixing a mistake" will even look like, and category-3 tools are the strongest case for a strict approval checkpoint
Leave the category undecided permanently, since it has no practical effect
Always assume every new tool is fully reversible by default
questions.explain: Deciding the undo category up front — not after an incident — tells you what recovery is even possible, and tools that can't be undone are exactly the ones that most need a strong approval checkpoint before they run.
